examples.label: PageRank
examples.title: Which people receive the most structural importance?
examples.description: Every incoming link contributes a share of its source score. This is a property of the directed network, not a judgment about the person.
examples.note: The browser computes a mathematical reference result for the baseline data. It does not invoke Oracle. SQL uses up to 1,000 iterations, tolerance 1e-10, damping 0.85 and normalization.
examples.sql:
SELECT person_id, person_name, ROUND(score, 6) AS pagerank_score
FROM GRAPH_TABLE (
  DBMS_OGA.PAGERANK(
    pgd_rel_graph,
    PROPERTY(VERTEX OUTPUT pr_score),
    1000, 1e-10, 0.85d, TRUE
  )
  MATCH (p IS person)
  COLUMNS (p.person_id AS person_id, p.name AS person_name,
           p.pr_score AS score)
)
ORDER BY score DESC, person_id;

examples.label: Personalized
examples.title: How does the ranking change when Alice is the focus?
examples.description: Personalized PageRank biases the ranking toward Alice. Compare the scores with the global PageRank result.
examples.note: The seed is a complete graph vertex identifier. PEOPLE is the element alias; person_id is the key. The query constructs the identifier for the connected graph owner.
examples.sql:
SELECT person_id, person_name, ROUND(score, 6) AS alice_score
FROM GRAPH_TABLE (
  DBMS_OGA.PERSONALIZED_PAGERANK(
    pgd_rel_graph,
    PROPERTY(VERTEX OUTPUT ppr_score),
    JSON_OBJECT(
      'GRAPH_OWNER' VALUE SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV', 'SESSION_USER'),
      'GRAPH_NAME' VALUE 'PGD_REL_GRAPH',
      'ELEM_TABLE' VALUE 'PEOPLE',
      'KEY_VALUE' VALUE JSON_OBJECT('PERSON_ID' VALUE 1)
      RETURNING JSON
    ),
    1000, 1e-10, 0.85d, TRUE
  )
  MATCH (p IS person)
  COLUMNS (p.person_id AS person_id, p.name AS person_name,
           p.ppr_score AS score)
)
ORDER BY score DESC, person_id;

examples.label: Seed set
examples.title: What if Alice and Carla are both the focus?
examples.description: PERSONALIZED_PAGERANK_SET gives equal preference to the two selected seed vertices. Its input is an array of graph vertex identifiers.
examples.note: Changing the input graph also changes the GRAPH_NAME in each seed identity. Query VERTEX_ID on that graph to obtain the correct identifiers.
examples.sql:
SELECT person_id, person_name, ROUND(score, 6) AS seed_set_score
FROM GRAPH_TABLE (
  DBMS_OGA.PERSONALIZED_PAGERANK_SET(
    pgd_rel_graph,
    PROPERTY(VERTEX OUTPUT set_score),
    JSON_ARRAY(
      JSON_OBJECT(
        'GRAPH_OWNER' VALUE SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV', 'SESSION_USER'),
        'GRAPH_NAME' VALUE 'PGD_REL_GRAPH',
        'ELEM_TABLE' VALUE 'PEOPLE',
        'KEY_VALUE' VALUE JSON_OBJECT('PERSON_ID' VALUE 1)
        RETURNING JSON
      ),
      JSON_OBJECT(
        'GRAPH_OWNER' VALUE SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV', 'SESSION_USER'),
        'GRAPH_NAME' VALUE 'PGD_REL_GRAPH',
        'ELEM_TABLE' VALUE 'PEOPLE',
        'KEY_VALUE' VALUE JSON_OBJECT('PERSON_ID' VALUE 3)
        RETURNING JSON
      )
      RETURNING JSON
    ),
    1000, 1e-10, 0.85d, TRUE
  )
  MATCH (p IS person)
  COLUMNS (p.person_id AS person_id, p.name AS person_name,
           p.set_score AS score)
)
ORDER BY score DESC, person_id;

examples.label: Components
examples.title: How many disconnected groups exist?
examples.description: WCC ignores arrow direction and groups all people connected by any chain of links. This dataset is one weakly connected component.
examples.note: The browser labels the single group for explanation. Oracle component IDs are opaque, may be non-contiguous, and can change between runs. WCC is not community detection.
examples.sql:
SELECT component_id, COUNT(*) AS people_count,
       LISTAGG(person_name, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY person_name) AS members
FROM GRAPH_TABLE (
  DBMS_OGA.WCC(
    pgd_rel_graph, PROPERTY(VERTEX OUTPUT component_id)
  )
  MATCH (p IS person)
  COLUMNS (p.name AS person_name, p.component_id AS component_id)
)
GROUP BY component_id
ORDER BY people_count DESC, members;

examples.label: Fewest hops
examples.title: What is the minimum number of outgoing steps from Alice?
examples.description: BELLMAN_FORD with hop_cost = 1 turns weighted shortest distance into minimum hop count. Unlike the earlier fixed two-hop pattern, it computes a minimum for every destination.
examples.note: Run the PGD_COST_GRAPH setup first. Output values are distances; the algorithm does not return a path sequence. Unreachable vertices receive positive infinity.
examples.sql:
SELECT person_id, person_name, min_hops
FROM GRAPH_TABLE (
  DBMS_OGA.BELLMAN_FORD(
    pgd_cost_graph,
    JSON_OBJECT(
      'GRAPH_OWNER' VALUE SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV', 'SESSION_USER'),
      'GRAPH_NAME' VALUE 'PGD_COST_GRAPH',
      'ELEM_TABLE' VALUE 'PEOPLE',
      'KEY_VALUE' VALUE JSON_OBJECT('PERSON_ID' VALUE 1)
      RETURNING JSON
    ),
    PROPERTY(EDGE INPUT hop_cost DEFAULT ON NULL 1),
    PROPERTY(VERTEX OUTPUT min_hops)
  )
  MATCH (p IS person)
  COLUMNS (p.person_id AS person_id, p.name AS person_name,
           p.min_hops AS min_hops)
)
ORDER BY person_id;

examples.label: Lowest cost
examples.title: Can a longer route cost less?
examples.description: Alice → Carla costs 9. Alice → Bob → Elena → Carla costs 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. The cheapest route to Carla takes three hops.
examples.note: These fictional effort values are expressions in graph metadata. No row is copied or updated. Oracle Bellman-Ford does not accept negative weights; expression inputs require DEFAULT ON NULL.
examples.sql:
SELECT person_id, person_name, min_effort
FROM GRAPH_TABLE (
  DBMS_OGA.BELLMAN_FORD(
    pgd_cost_graph,
    JSON_OBJECT(
      'GRAPH_OWNER' VALUE SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV', 'SESSION_USER'),
      'GRAPH_NAME' VALUE 'PGD_COST_GRAPH',
      'ELEM_TABLE' VALUE 'PEOPLE',
      'KEY_VALUE' VALUE JSON_OBJECT('PERSON_ID' VALUE 1)
      RETURNING JSON
    ),
    PROPERTY(EDGE INPUT effort DEFAULT ON NULL 1),
    PROPERTY(VERTEX OUTPUT min_effort)
  )
  MATCH (p IS person)
  COLUMNS (p.person_id AS person_id, p.name AS person_name,
           p.min_effort AS min_effort)
)
ORDER BY person_id;

cost_ddl:
CREATE OR REPLACE PROPERTY GRAPH pgd_cost_graph
  VERTEX TABLES (
    pgd_person AS people KEY (person_id)
      LABEL person PROPERTIES (person_id, person_name AS name, city)
  )
  EDGE TABLES (
    pgd_knows AS links KEY (edge_id)
      SOURCE KEY (src_id) REFERENCES people (person_id)
      DESTINATION KEY (dst_id) REFERENCES people (person_id)
      LABEL knows PROPERTIES (
        edge_id, since_year,
        1 AS hop_cost,
        CASE edge_id
          WHEN 101 THEN 1 WHEN 102 THEN 9 WHEN 103 THEN 2
          WHEN 104 THEN 1 WHEN 105 THEN 1 WHEN 106 THEN 1
          WHEN 107 THEN 1 ELSE 1
        END AS effort
      )
  )
  OPTIONS (ENFORCED MODE);
pattern_query:
SELECT DISTINCT target_name, ROUND(score, 6) AS pagerank_score
FROM GRAPH_TABLE (
  DBMS_OGA.PAGERANK(
    pgd_rel_graph, PROPERTY(VERTEX OUTPUT pr_score),
    1000, 1e-10, 0.85d, TRUE
  )
  MATCH (a IS person)-[e1 IS knows]->(b IS person)
                     -[e2 IS knows]->(c IS person)
  WHERE a.person_id = 1
  COLUMNS (c.name AS target_name, c.pr_score AS score)
)
ORDER BY pagerank_score DESC, target_name;
